lesson.title: High-availability multi-AZ application design
lesson.why: Placing two servers in different zones is only the beginning of availability design. Shared dependencies, insufficient surviving capacity, and synchronized retries can still cause a complete outage.
lesson.what: Design a hypothetical multi-zone order service with stateless compute, resilient data, readiness checks, failure headroom, and bounded recovery behavior.

concepts.name: Trace the entire request path
concepts.body: DNS, ingress, application compute, authentication, databases, queues, and outbound dependencies all contribute to availability. Redundancy in one tier cannot repair a single point of failure elsewhere. Record each component's failure domain and whether its data or control plane is needed during recovery.

concepts.name: Capacity must survive failure
concepts.body: Reactive scaling takes time, so surviving zones need enough preexisting capacity for immediate demand. Overlap during deployment can consume that headroom. Evaluate traffic skew and expensive requests instead of assuming every request has identical cost or every zone receives an equal share.

concepts.name: State needs explicit failover semantics
concepts.body: Stateless application instances simplify replacement, but database replication, session storage, and queues have their own consistency and recovery behavior. Synchronous replication can protect committed data within its scope, while failover still causes connection disruption and possibly ambiguous transaction outcomes.

concepts.name: Recovery can amplify overload
concepts.body: Retries, cache misses, reconnection storms, and health-check flapping can overload surviving dependencies. Use deadlines, bounded exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency, and load shedding where appropriate. A failover test must check user outcomes, not merely whether a replacement instance exists.

e2e: Define service success, latency, failure scope, and acceptable recovery time.
Draw the request path with component placement and shared dependencies.
Calculate one-zone-loss capacity and choose state replication consistent with correctness needs.
Define meaningful health checks, draining, deadlines, and duplicate-safe retries.
Rehearse a scoped failure in an approved environment and revise assumptions using measured outcomes.

tasks.name: Find a hidden single point
steps: Sketch two-zone application compute with one database, one outbound gateway, and in-memory sessions.
Mark which components still bind availability to a single location or process; propose separate remedies rather than just adding web replicas.

tasks.name: Calculate failure headroom
steps: Assume six instances across three zones, two each, with safe capacity 75 requests/second per instance and demand 280.
One-zone loss leaves four instances or 300 requests/second, only 20 headroom. Losing one more instance during deployment leaves 225 and fails the requirement.

tasks.name: Trace a retry storm
steps: A database failover causes 1,000 clients to reconnect and retry immediately. Add jitter, deadlines, and a bounded retry budget.
Use stable order IDs so an uncertain commit is checked before another order is created.

tasks.name: Write failure-test acceptance
steps: Define synthetic request success, p95 latency, duplicate-order checks, and maximum recovery interval for a hypothetical drill.
Do not run a fault injection here. Offline topology does not prove actual failover, capacity, or cloud authorization.

key_terms: Failure domain: boundary within which failures can correlate.
Headroom: spare capacity beyond current demand.
Readiness: ability to accept useful work.
Load shedding: rejecting lower-priority work to protect capacity.
Ambiguous commit: unknown transaction result after communication failure.
lesson.safety: Do not disable resources or inject faults. Extra replicas, replicated storage, logs, and transfer cost money; real drills require authorization, rollback, and customer-impact limits.
cleanup: Keep the dependency map and arithmetic.
No resources were created or interrupted; future drills need explicit restoration and retained-log review.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a service spans three zones but fails when one zone disappears during deployment. How would you explain and investigate?
interview_points: Calculate combined zone-loss and deployment headroom.
Inspect shared state and outbound dependencies.
Measure retry and reconnection amplification.
Validate user outcomes and idempotent recovery rather than replica count alone.

architecture/high-availability-multi-az-.core: Multi-zone availability is an end-to-end property. Map shared dependencies, reserve surviving capacity, design state failover, and bound retry amplification. Zone diversity alone is not proof of resilience.

storyboard.title: A zone loss collides with deployment draining
storyboard.objective: Connect overlapping disruptions to insufficient surviving capacity.

scenes.title: Normal headroom
scenes.caption: The fleet can carry current demand with spare capacity.
scenes.narration: Requests are balanced across zones and use an external database, avoiding dependence on one application's local session state.

scenes.title: Two disruptions overlap
scenes.caption: Deployment draining consumes zone-loss reserve.
scenes.narration: A zone fails while another instance drains for deployment, leaving less usable capacity than the request load requires.

scenes.title: Recover within a bounded load
scenes.caption: Pause rollout and prevent retry amplification.
scenes.narration: Operators stop draining, protect the database with bounded retries, and restore ready capacity while measuring successful orders and latency.

lesson.title: Multi-region recovery versus active-active trade-offs
lesson.why: A second region can improve disaster recovery while adding conflict, consistency, cost, and operational complexity. Active-active is not automatically the safest or simplest answer.
lesson.what: Compare backup restore, pilot light, warm standby, and active-active for a fictional order platform using explicit RPO, RTO, and data-authority assumptions.

concepts.name: Recovery strategies maintain different readiness
concepts.body: Backup restore retains recoverable data but may require substantial infrastructure recreation. Pilot light keeps essential components ready; warm standby runs a reduced-capacity environment. Active-active serves from multiple locations. These labels describe patterns, not guaranteed recovery times or zero-loss promises.

concepts.name: Replication has correctness trade-offs
concepts.body: Asynchronous cross-region replication can lag, creating a potential data-loss window on forced failover. Synchronous coordination can increase write latency and reduce availability during partitions. Multi-writer systems need conflict and uniqueness rules that fit business invariants, not merely eventual record convergence.

concepts.name: Traffic routing does not establish authority
concepts.body: DNS or global routing changes where clients connect, but cached answers and existing connections can persist. Fence the old writer when transferring authority to prevent split brain. A reachable secondary should not accept writes until data and ownership decisions are explicit.

concepts.name: Failback is another migration
concepts.body: After recovery-region writes begin, returning to the original region requires reconciliation and controlled routing. Backups, key access, quotas, artifacts, and identity must exist where recovery runs. Rehearsals should include failback and degraded dependencies, not only a successful regional switch.

e2e: Define regional failure scenarios, acceptable data loss, and useful-service recovery deadline.
Choose a readiness pattern and replication semantics consistent with business invariants.
Provision or document recovery dependencies and a write-fencing mechanism.
Use explicit decision gates for data checkpoint, authority transfer, capacity, and traffic movement.
Rehearse both failover and failback with reconciliation and measured client behavior.

tasks.name: Choose a strategy by objective
steps: Compare a low-traffic internal archive tolerating hours of recovery with an order service needing rapid restoration.
Consider backup restore for the first and evaluate warm standby or more active readiness for the second, including operating cost and correctness.

tasks.name: Calculate a recovery budget
steps: Assume detection five minutes, decision three, database promotion four, scaling six, and verification two, executed sequentially.
Modeled recovery is 20 minutes. A 15-minute objective is not met; overlap requires proven dependencies rather than simply subtracting steps.

tasks.name: Assess replication lag
tasks.goal: Separate lag from proven lost transactions.
steps: At failure, the secondary's last applied checkpoint is 90 seconds behind the source's last observed checkpoint.
Report a potential window requiring transaction reconciliation, not an invented exact lost-order count or zero-loss guarantee.

tasks.name: Plan failback safely
steps: List write fencing, data reconciliation, endpoint updates, client retries, and a rollback checkpoint before returning authority.
This paper rehearsal does not prove actual replication, regional capacity, or IAM behavior.

key_terms: RPO: acceptable data-loss window.
RTO: target time to restore useful service.
Pilot light: minimal recovery foundation kept ready.
Warm standby: reduced-capacity running recovery environment.
Split brain: competing writers acting as authoritative owners.
lesson.safety: Do not fail over services or copy real data. Secondary infrastructure, replication, backups, and transfer can be expensive and subject to residency constraints; drills require approval.
cleanup: Keep the recovery budget and authority diagram.
No traffic routes, databases, or regional resources were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, DNS now points to a secondary region but both databases accept orders. What is the immediate correctness concern?
interview_points: Prevent split-brain writes with explicit fencing.
Establish the authoritative checkpoint and reconcile differences.
Account for cached clients and existing connections.
Plan failback as a data migration, not just another DNS edit.

architecture/multi-region-recovery-versu.core: Multi-region design trades readiness cost against recovery time and consistency. Routing does not determine write authority. Define fencing, lag handling, dependency readiness, and failback before claiming recovery objectives.

storyboard.title: Regional routing changes before write authority is fenced
storyboard.objective: Show the split-brain risk in an incomplete failover.

scenes.title: Single authoritative region
scenes.caption: Replication prepares a recovery copy.
scenes.narration: The original region accepts writes while the secondary follows a documented replication checkpoint and remains ready for a controlled transition.

scenes.title: Both regions accept writes
scenes.caption: Routing alone does not prevent competing authority.
scenes.narration: Some clients retain old connections while new clients reach the recovery region, creating conflicting writes if the original writer is not fenced.

scenes.title: Establish one authority
scenes.caption: Fencing and reconciliation precede stable recovery.
scenes.narration: Operators apply the approved fencing mechanism, reconcile accepted changes, and verify client routing before declaring recovery or planning failback.

lesson.title: System design requirements estimation and bottlenecks
lesson.why: A diagram without demand assumptions cannot explain why it will work. Estimation helps identify the first bottleneck, but averages and unsupported precision can hide overload risk.
lesson.what: Size a fictional event-ingestion service using functional requirements, latency objectives, arrival rates, concurrency, storage growth, and failure scenarios.

concepts.name: Requirements define the design space
concepts.body: Separate user actions from quality attributes such as latency, availability, consistency, retention, and privacy. State which requirements are hard constraints and which are preferences. Clarify peak periods, geographic users, and operational ownership before selecting databases or queues.

concepts.name: Use dimensional arithmetic
concepts.body: Translate business activity into requests per second, bytes per event, retention volume, and concurrent work. Keep decimal GB distinct from binary GiB and record every multiplier. An estimate should expose assumptions so reviewers can challenge them rather than appear precise by using many digits.

concepts.name: Bottlenecks depend on work mix
concepts.body: Request count alone misses different query costs, payload sizes, and cache behavior. CPU, memory, disk, network, locks, connections, and downstream quotas can each dominate. Little's Law relates average work in the system to arrival rate and average time under appropriate stable conditions.

concepts.name: Overload needs a response policy
concepts.body: Queues absorb bursts but can grow without bound if arrivals exceed processing. Backpressure, bounded queues, admission control, and graceful degradation protect useful service. Retrying every failure immediately increases load; define deadlines and prioritize work according to user impact.

e2e: Write the user workflow and rank measurable quality requirements.
Estimate peak arrivals, payload size, operation mix, and retention from explicit assumptions.
Translate demand into concurrency, storage, and dependency budgets.
Identify the first limiting resource and choose a bounded overload strategy.
Validate with representative tests later and revise the model rather than treating estimates as benchmarks.

tasks.name: Clarify a vague requirement
steps: Replace 'fast and scalable ingestion' with an assumed peak rate, acceptable acknowledgement latency, retention period, and loss tolerance.
Mark every value hypothetical and list the stakeholder who must confirm it.

tasks.name: Calculate storage and concurrency
steps: Assume 100 events/second, 2,000 bytes/event, and 0.2-second average processing time. Average concurrent processing is 20.
Daily raw data is 100 x 2,000 x 86,400 = 17,280,000,000 bytes, or 17.28 decimal GB, before indexes, replication, and compression.

tasks.name: Find an unstable queue
steps: Producers send 100 events/second but consumers finish 80. After ten minutes, modeled backlog grows by 20 x 600 = 12,000 events.
Explain why a larger queue delays failure without solving sustained undercapacity.

tasks.name: Design a validation plan
steps: Choose tests for expensive events, cold caches, downstream slowdown, and recovery backlog, with explicit error and latency gates.
No load generator is run here. Offline estimates do not prove real cloud throughput or authorization.

key_terms: Functional requirement: behavior the system must provide.
Quality attribute: measurable property such as latency or availability.
Arrival rate: new work entering per unit time.
Concurrency: work simultaneously in progress.
Backpressure: signal or mechanism slowing upstream production.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic volumes and no production load tests. Oversizing wastes money; unbounded testing can create charges and outages. Do not invent benchmark results from arithmetic.
cleanup: Retain the assumption table and units.
No datasets or resources were created; discard scratch diagrams if not needed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a design meets average throughput but collapses during bursts. What estimates and controls are missing?
interview_points: Model peak rate and expensive request mix.
Include concurrency, queue growth, and dependency limits.
Use bounded admission and retries.
Validate assumptions with representative evidence, not invented benchmarks.

architecture/system-design-requirements-.core: System design begins with measurable requirements and explicit units. Estimate concurrency and retained bytes, identify work-mix bottlenecks, and bound overload. A queue absorbs bursts but cannot fix permanently inadequate processing.

storyboard.title: An ingestion queue grows faster than workers can drain it
storyboard.objective: Connect arrival rate, completion rate, and backpressure.

scenes.title: Stable flow
scenes.caption: Average completion capacity covers incoming work.
scenes.narration: The service receives events and drains them fast enough that normal fluctuations do not cause sustained backlog growth.

scenes.title: Arrival exceeds completion
scenes.caption: A larger queue does not create processing capacity.
scenes.narration: Producers sustain a higher rate than workers can complete, so queued work accumulates and waiting time rises.

scenes.title: Bound demand and restore capacity
scenes.caption: Backpressure protects deadlines and useful work.
scenes.narration: The design limits admission or slows producers while addressing the worker bottleneck, then verifies backlog recovery under realistic event costs.

lesson.title: Monolith microservices and event-driven trade-offs
lesson.why: Splitting code into services can improve independent delivery or create distributed failure modes without useful autonomy. Architecture style should follow team boundaries, change patterns, and consistency needs.
lesson.what: Compare a modular monolith, synchronous microservices, and event-driven collaboration for a fictional commerce system, including operational cost and data ownership.

concepts.name: A monolith can be modular
concepts.body: A single deployable unit can enforce clear internal modules and database boundaries while retaining local calls and straightforward transactions. It is not necessarily unstructured. Shared deployment and scaling may become constraints, but splitting too early can add networking and operations before boundaries are understood.

concepts.name: Microservices trade local simplicity for autonomy
concepts.body: Independent services can own data and deploy separately when contracts and teams support that autonomy. Cross-service calls introduce partial failure, latency, version skew, and distributed tracing needs. Many separately deployed components sharing one tightly coupled database can become a distributed monolith.

concepts.name: Events decouple time, not responsibility
concepts.body: Publishing facts allows consumers to react independently and tolerate temporary unavailability. Event schemas, ordering, duplicates, and eventual consistency become explicit concerns. A broker does not automatically make producer database updates and event publication atomic; an outbox or equivalent coordination may be required.

concepts.name: Operational readiness changes the answer
concepts.body: More services require deployment pipelines, observability, ownership, access control, incident response, and capacity management. Count on-call and coordination costs alongside compute. Choose a reversible boundary with clear value rather than treating service count as a maturity metric.

e2e: Map business capabilities, change frequency, data invariants, and team ownership.
Start with explicit module boundaries and identify a proven autonomy or scaling constraint.
Choose synchronous or asynchronous interaction according to immediate consistency and timing needs.
Define contracts, data ownership, retry behavior, and observability before extraction.
Validate the first boundary and retain a practical rollback or reintegration path.

tasks.name: Compare two team contexts
steps: A three-person team changes one product weekly; a larger organization has independently owned billing and catalog capabilities.
Explain why a modular monolith may fit the first while selective service boundaries could benefit the second.

tasks.name: Calculate call-chain latency
steps: Assume a request makes four sequential remote calls taking 25 ms each plus 20 ms local work.
Modeled latency is 120 ms before retries or queueing. Parallelization is valid only for independent calls; do not subtract dependencies to improve the diagram.

tasks.name: Find the dual-write gap
steps: An order commits to a database, then the process crashes before publishing its event.
Propose a transactional outbox recorded with the order and an idempotent publisher/consumer path instead of assuming two separate writes are atomic.

tasks.name: Write an extraction gate
steps: Choose catalog as a hypothetical boundary and require independent ownership, contract tests, data migration, monitoring, and rollback.
These offline designs do not prove distributed behavior, throughput, or a real team's readiness.

key_terms: Modular monolith: one deployment with enforced internal boundaries.
Microservice: independently operated service around a capability.
Distributed monolith: separate deployments retaining tight coupling.
Eventual consistency: convergence without immediate global agreement.
Outbox: durable event intent committed with business data.
lesson.safety: Do not split production services or publish real events. Extra deployments, brokers, transfer, telemetry, and on-call load have costs; preserve transaction correctness during experiments.
cleanup: Retain the capability and contract map.
No services, schemas, or broker resources were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a team deploys twenty services together and shares one schema. What benefits of microservices might be missing?
interview_points: Independent deployment and data ownership may be absent.
Inspect synchronous and schema coupling.
Compare operational overhead with a modular monolith.
Extract only justified boundaries with contract and migration evidence.

architecture/monolith-microservices-and-.core: Architecture styles exchange local simplicity for autonomy and asynchronous coordination. A modular monolith can be deliberate; microservices need independent ownership and contracts. Events still require duplicate handling and atomic publication intent.
objectives: Identify distributed coupling and dual writes

storyboard.title: An order commit loses its separately published event
storyboard.objective: Show why event-driven design needs atomic publication intent.

scenes.title: Order is accepted
scenes.caption: Business state must become durable.
scenes.narration: The order module commits its accepted state, and fulfillment depends on learning that fact through an event contract.

scenes.title: Separate publication fails
scenes.caption: Two unrelated writes are not one transaction.
scenes.narration: A crash between database commit and event publication can leave fulfillment unaware of a valid order if no durable intent exists.

scenes.title: Relay from an outbox
scenes.caption: Durable intent and idempotency close the recovery gap.
scenes.narration: The design commits event intent with the order, then relays it with retries while consumers deduplicate repeated delivery.

lesson.title: API design versioning authentication and rate limiting
lesson.why: An API is a long-lived contract between independently changing systems. Clear resource semantics, authorization, compatibility, and overload behavior prevent fragile clients and unsafe retries.
lesson.what: Design a fictional orders API with stable identifiers, object-level access checks, versioning, pagination, idempotency, and explicit throttling behavior.

concepts.name: Resources and operations need semantics
concepts.body: Use stable resource identifiers and consistent HTTP methods and status codes. Reads should not mutate business state. Pagination needs a documented order and cursor or offset behavior under concurrent changes. A transport-success response should accurately represent whether work completed or was merely accepted.

concepts.name: Authentication is not object authorization
concepts.body: Validate token issuer, audience, expiry, and other required claims using supported mechanisms. Then verify the principal may access the specific order or tenant. A valid user token does not authorize every object ID; rate limiting and hidden URLs do not replace access control.

concepts.name: Compatibility includes client assumptions
concepts.body: Removing fields, changing types, changing meaning, or narrowing accepted input can break clients. Even additive enum values can surprise strict clients. Version changes need a migration and deprecation policy, observability of usage, and contract tests rather than an arbitrary new path prefix alone.

concepts.name: Retries and limits form a contract
concepts.body: Use bounded retry guidance and appropriate status signaling for transient overload. Idempotency keys protect supported mutations when responses are lost. Rate and burst controls should define scope and fairness; distributed enforcement may be approximate, so it is not inherently a hard billing or security guarantee.

e2e: Define order resources, schemas, errors, and ownership rules with client stakeholders.
Specify authentication and per-object authorization before adding convenience endpoints.
Choose pagination and versioning rules that tolerate expected data and client evolution.
Define idempotency and overload responses with deadlines and bounded client retries.
Validate positive, negative, compatibility, duplicate, and pagination cases using synthetic data.

tasks.name: Write an authorization matrix
steps: Create fictional users A and B with one order each. A may read A's order but not B's; an unauthenticated caller may read neither.
Make this a server-side ownership rule rather than trusting a client-supplied user ID.

tasks.name: Calculate a bounded page count
steps: Assume an immutable snapshot of 235 orders and page size 50. Expected pages are ceiling(235/50) = five, with 35 orders on the last page.
Explain that concurrent insertions require defined cursor or snapshot semantics; the arithmetic alone does not prevent duplicates or omissions.

tasks.name: Review a version change
steps: An API changes status from a string enum to an object and introduces a new required request field.
Classify both as potentially breaking and require contract tests and a migration window instead of labeling the release backward compatible.

tasks.name: Trace a lost response
steps: A POST creates order X but its response is lost. Retry with the same supported idempotency key and retrieve the existing result.
These offline cases do not prove real token verification, rate enforcement, or backend transactions.

key_terms: Resource: stable API-addressable business entity.
Object authorization: permission check on a particular entity.
Cursor: continuation marker for paginated results.
Breaking change: change invalidating an existing client contract.
Idempotency key: identifier for one logical mutation.
lesson.safety: Do not expose endpoints or use real bearer tokens. API traffic, retries, logs, and abuse can incur costs; redact request data and preserve authorization in mocks.
cleanup: No API deployments, keys, or user records were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an authenticated user can change the order ID in a URL and read another customer's order. Why does token validation not solve this?
interview_points: Authentication establishes identity, not object ownership.
Enforce tenant and object authorization server-side.
Test cross-user negative cases.
Do not substitute rate limits, obscured IDs, or client checks for authorization.

architecture/api-design-versioning-authe.core: APIs need stable semantics, object-level authorization, compatibility policy, and bounded overload behavior. Authentication is not ownership. Pagination and mutation retries require explicit correctness contracts.

storyboard.title: An authenticated request targets another user's order
storyboard.objective: Separate identity validation from object authorization.

scenes.title: Identity validates
scenes.caption: The token identifies a real customer.
scenes.narration: The API validates the request's token and establishes the caller identity before looking up the requested order.

scenes.title: Ownership differs
scenes.caption: A valid token does not authorize arbitrary object IDs.
scenes.narration: The supplied order belongs to another customer, so returning it would violate the API's object-level access boundary.

scenes.title: Deny without leaking data
scenes.caption: Server-side checks preserve the resource boundary.
scenes.narration: The API rejects the unauthorized lookup using its documented error contract and verifies that legitimate owner access still succeeds.

lesson.title: Migration planning strangler patterns and rollback
lesson.why: Replacing a large system in one cutover concentrates risk. Incremental migration can reduce that risk only when routing, data ownership, observability, and rollback are designed together.
lesson.what: Plan a strangler-style migration of a fictional product catalog from a legacy application to a new service, preserving the client interface and authoritative data rules.

concepts.name: A routing facade enables gradual replacement
concepts.body: The strangler pattern directs selected functionality to a new implementation while remaining capabilities stay on the legacy system. Choose a cohesive boundary and keep the public contract stable. The facade itself becomes critical infrastructure requiring monitoring, capacity, and recovery planning.

concepts.name: Data ownership is the hardest boundary
concepts.body: A new service reading old tables may preserve coupling even after traffic moves. Dual writes can diverge when one destination fails. Define an authoritative writer, a supported synchronization method, and reconciliation before allowing both systems to modify the same business facts.

concepts.name: Shadow traffic needs side-effect control
concepts.body: Comparing old and new responses can expose behavior differences before cutover. Mirroring mutating requests can create duplicate emails, orders, or payments unless effects are disabled or isolated. Scrub sensitive data and compare outputs at an understood consistency point rather than demanding byte equality from nondeterministic fields.

concepts.name: Rollback has a data frontier
concepts.body: Before the new system accepts unique writes, routing rollback may be simple. Afterward, those writes must be preserved or reconciled before returning authority. Database expansion and contraction should preserve old-client compatibility during transition; destructive schema removal belongs after the rollback window closes.

e2e: Inventory legacy contracts, dependencies, business invariants, and migration constraints.
Select one capability and introduce a monitored routing boundary.
Prepare compatible data synchronization and synthetic shadow comparisons without external side effects.
Move a bounded traffic slice using explicit correctness and latency gates.
Retain rollback routing and data reconciliation until decommissioning criteria are verified.

tasks.name: Choose the first slice
steps: Compare extracting read-only catalog search with replacing checkout, payment, and inventory together.
Prefer investigating the smaller catalog slice because its contract and side effects are easier to validate, while documenting shared data dependencies.

tasks.name: Calculate a canary split
steps: Assume 2,000 eligible requests per minute and a 5% canary share. Expected new-service traffic is 100 requests/minute; legacy receives 1,900.
A stable cohort strategy avoids inconsistent user routing; these counts are expectations, not real routing test results.

tasks.name: Review unsafe mirroring
steps: A proposal mirrors order POST requests to both implementations with live payment integration enabled.
Reject it. Use synthetic or isolated side-effect-free comparisons, and never treat shadow traffic as permission to double-charge.

tasks.name: Design post-write rollback
steps: The new catalog accepts 40 edits before a defect appears. Fence writes and reconcile those edits before switching writer authority back.
This offline plan does not prove migration completeness, route behavior, or cloud permissions.

key_terms: Strangler pattern: incremental replacement behind a stable interface.
Facade: routing boundary selecting an implementation.
Shadow traffic: copied requests used for comparison rather than authoritative service.
Write authority: system responsible for accepted data changes.
Expand-contract: schema evolution preserving compatibility before removing old structure.
lesson.safety: Do not route real traffic or copy customer payloads. Dual operation, synchronization, and telemetry add cost; mirrored mutations can create irreversible side effects.
cleanup: Keep migration gates and synthetic comparison cases.
No services or data were migrated; future decommissioning requires explicit dependency and retention approval.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a new service accepted writes during a canary and then failed. Why is switching all traffic back not necessarily a safe rollback?
interview_points: New writes may exist only in the new authority.
Fence writers and reconcile data first.
Keep old-schema compatibility through the rollback window.
Validate invariants before decommissioning either system.

architecture/migration-planning-strangle.core: Strangler migration moves one capability behind a stable routing boundary. Safe rollout requires explicit data authority, side-effect-free comparisons, and rollback that preserves writes accepted by the new system.

storyboard.title: A catalog canary crosses the rollback data frontier
storyboard.objective: Show why accepted writes complicate routing rollback.

scenes.title: Small capability canary
scenes.caption: Most requests remain on the legacy path.
scenes.narration: The facade directs a bounded cohort to the new catalog while retaining the stable client interface and legacy fallback.

scenes.title: Defect follows new writes
scenes.caption: Routing reversal alone could hide accepted edits.
scenes.narration: The canary encounters a defect after accepting unique catalog changes, creating data that the legacy implementation may not yet contain.

scenes.title: Reconcile before authority reversal
scenes.caption: Rollback preserves business state.
scenes.narration: Operators fence writes, reconcile accepted edits, verify invariants, and only then return authoritative traffic to the compatible legacy path.

lesson.title: Technical decision records and stakeholder communication
lesson.why: Future engineers need to understand why an architecture was chosen, not merely see its current shape. A good decision record preserves context, rejected options, consequences, and uncertainty.
lesson.what: Write an architecture decision record for a hypothetical queue-backed export service, then communicate the same decision appropriately to engineers, product owners, and finance.

concepts.name: Record significant decisions
concepts.body: An ADR captures context, constraints, options, decision, rationale, and consequences for an architecturally important choice. It is not a transcript of every discussion or a marketing justification. Include the status and decision owner so readers distinguish proposed ideas from accepted commitments.

concepts.name: Constraints precede scoring
concepts.body: A hard requirement such as data residency or a recovery objective can disqualify an option regardless of its weighted score. Scores summarize judgment, not objective truth. Show weights, assumptions, evidence quality, and sensitivity instead of hiding a preferred answer behind arithmetic.

concepts.name: Consequences include disadvantages
concepts.body: Explain new operational work, migration cost, lock-in, failure modes, and skills required by the selected option. State what evidence would trigger reconsideration. A record that lists only advantages prevents informed future change and can mislead stakeholders about ongoing ownership.

concepts.name: History should remain traceable
concepts.body: Accepted decisions should retain their historical rationale. When a decision changes, create a superseding record and link the relationship rather than rewriting the past as if the new choice was always obvious. Tailor summaries to stakeholder concerns without changing factual claims or concealing uncertainty.

e2e: Define the decision question, affected stakeholders, and hard constraints.
Compare a small set of credible options with evidence and explicit unknowns.
Record the chosen option, trade-offs, owner, status, and reconsideration triggers.
Communicate implementation effects to engineering and value/cost effects to business stakeholders.
Review outcomes later and supersede the record if new evidence changes the decision.

tasks.name: Frame the decision
steps: Replace 'use queues because they scale' with a decision about handling exports that exceed an interactive request deadline.
List completion-time, durability, ownership, and cost constraints before naming products.

tasks.name: Work a decision matrix
steps: Assume option A scores reliability 4 and cost 2; B scores 3 and 5. Weights are 0.7 and 0.3.
A scores 3.4; B scores 3.6. If B violates required residency, reject B despite its higher score. These fictional scores are judgments, not measurements.

tasks.name: Write consequences
steps: For a queue-backed export, record worker ownership, duplicate handling, status API, retry policy, and added monitoring cost.
Include delayed completion as a user-experience trade-off rather than presenting asynchronous processing as unconditionally better.

tasks.name: Communicate and supersede
tasks.goal: Preserve one factual decision across audiences.
steps: Write a technical summary about idempotency and a business summary about reliable export completion; label estimates in both.
Draft a trigger for reconsideration, such as a changed deadline. This offline record is not production evidence or stakeholder approval.

key_terms: ADR: architecture decision record.
Constraint: requirement that limits acceptable choices.
Trade-off: benefit obtained with a corresponding disadvantage.
Decision owner: accountable person or role accepting the choice.
Superseding record: later decision linked to an earlier accepted one.
lesson.safety: Use hypothetical systems and public assumptions. Do not include private contracts, credentials, customer details, or fabricated approvals; implementation costs require a separate authorized decision.
cleanup: Keep the fictional ADR content if useful for practice.
No repository decision history or stakeholder communication was changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, new evidence invalidates an accepted architecture choice. How do you communicate a change without rewriting history or blaming the original team?
interview_points: Preserve original context and evidence.
Explain what changed and its consequences.
Create a linked superseding decision.
Assign migration ownership and acknowledge remaining uncertainty.

architecture/technical-decision-records-.core: ADRs preserve why a significant choice was made, including alternatives, constraints, drawbacks, and evidence. Hard constraints outrank scoring. Supersede accepted records transparently and tailor summaries without changing facts.

storyboard.title: A higher-scoring option violates a hard constraint
storyboard.objective: Separate decision arithmetic from acceptable design boundaries.

scenes.title: Compare credible options
scenes.caption: Scores summarize explicitly stated judgments.
scenes.narration: The team compares reliability and cost with documented weights while preserving the evidence and assumptions behind each score.

scenes.title: A hard constraint fails
scenes.caption: The highest numeric score is not automatically acceptable.
scenes.narration: One option scores well but violates required residency, so its attractive aggregate number cannot justify selecting it.

scenes.title: Record the feasible trade-off
scenes.caption: The decision preserves both rationale and disadvantages.
scenes.narration: The ADR selects an acceptable option, records its operational consequences, and names evidence that would trigger a future superseding decision.

lesson.title: Behavioral interviews using honest evidence and reflection
lesson.why: Distinguish personal actions, team outcomes, and uncertainty. Inventing leadership or numerical impact undermines trust and prevents meaningful reflection.
lesson.what: Practice situation, task, action, result, and learning using an explicitly hypothetical incident. Adapt the structure only to experiences you actually had.

concepts.name: Use structure without manufacturing experience
concepts.body: Situation gives context; task states responsibility; action identifies your work; result describes observed outcomes. Reflect on what you would change. Labs, coursework, and volunteering are valid evidence when labeled honestly rather than presented as production employment.

concepts.name: Separate contribution from team achievement
concepts.body: Use 'I' for your decisions and work and 'we' for shared outcomes. Credit collaborators and describe constraints. If you only observed an incident, explain what you learned rather than claiming command of the response. Clarify hypothetical reasoning when discussing something you have not done.

concepts.name: Quantify only supported outcomes
concepts.body: Use measurements with a known baseline, period, and source when permitted to share them. A percentage without a denominator can mislead, and correlation is not proof your action caused improvement. If metrics are unavailable, describe verifiable qualitative outcomes and explicitly state the limitation.

concepts.name: Reflect without blame or disclosure
concepts.body: Discuss contributing system conditions and improvements rather than attacking individuals. Explain what failed, how you sought feedback, and what changed afterward. Remove customer identities, credentials, private incidents, and confidential financial details while preserving enough technical context to demonstrate reasoning.

e2e: Choose a genuine experience appropriate to the question, or clearly label a practice scenario hypothetical.
List your actual responsibility, collaborators, constraints, and permitted evidence.
Draft specific actions with reasoning and alternatives rather than a list of tool names.
State observed outcomes and limitations, then identify a concrete learning or follow-up.
Practice a concise delivery and answer follow-up questions without inflating ownership or certainty.

tasks.name: Classify evidence honestly
steps: Compare personally fixing a local lab, observing a team's outage, and leading an approved production response.
Write an opening sentence for each that states the real role and environment; do not promote a lab into a production claim.

tasks.name: Work a hypothetical impact calculation
steps: In an invented practice dataset, median build duration falls from ten to eight minutes. Relative reduction is (10 - 8) / 10 = 20%.
State that this is synthetic arithmetic, not your achievement. For a real story, require comparable measurements and acknowledge other concurrent changes.

tasks.name: Draft a scoped response
steps: Using only a hypothetical failed release, outline context, assigned validation task, evidence you would inspect, rollback recommendation, and follow-up.
Use conditional wording throughout. The exercise rehearses reasoning and does not establish professional experience or test results.

tasks.name: Practice reflection and redaction
steps: Replace a blame statement with a system-focused observation about missing tests or unclear ownership, then propose an actionable improvement.
Remove names and sensitive details. Identify one question you would answer with 'I do not know' rather than inventing an explanation.

key_terms: STAR: situation, task, action, result response structure.
Attribution: accurate assignment of contribution and outcome.
Baseline: reference measurement used for comparison.
Reflection: explanation of learning and future change.
Blameless analysis: investigation focused on contributing conditions rather than personal punishment.
lesson.safety: Practice locally without sending responses or accessing private incident records. Preparation costs time but needs no paid cloud resources; never disclose confidential evidence or fabricate credentials and achievements.
cleanup: Discard sensitive drafts and keep only appropriately anonymized notes.
The hypothetical numbers and scenario must remain labeled synthetic if reused.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an interviewer asks about an outage you observed but did not lead. How would you answer honestly while showing useful judgment?
interview_points: State your actual observer or contributor role.
Describe verified observations and distinguish proposed actions.
Credit the response team and avoid private details.
Explain learning and limits without inventing impact metrics.

architecture/behavioral-interviews-using.core: Attribute genuine evidence accurately. Label labs and hypotheses, protect confidentiality, and reflect without blame.
objectives: Build an honest structured interview response
prerequisites: One genuine learning or teamwork experience

storyboard.title: An interview story preserves honest contribution
storyboard.objective: Show how evidence and reflection replace inflated claims.

scenes.title: Select an authentic example
scenes.caption: The story begins with its real environment and role.
scenes.narration: The candidate chooses an experience they actually had and identifies their own responsibility separately from the team's broader work.

scenes.title: An unsupported claim appears
scenes.caption: Missing evidence is not permission to invent impact.
scenes.narration: A draft implies leadership or numerical improvement that the available observations do not establish, making the response misleading.

scenes.title: Revise with honest reflection
scenes.caption: Clear limits strengthen rather than weaken credibility.
scenes.narration: The response states the actual contribution, credits collaborators, labels uncertainty, and explains a concrete lesson without exposing confidential details.
